I have been trying to learn the art of wandering again. Not hiking with a destination, not walking to get steps, not even strolling to clear my head. Just wandering: leaving the house without a map, without a podcast, without the leash of a reason. It is harder than it sounds. The moment I step outside, my hand twitches toward my phone. My brain starts composing a to-do list. I catch myself walking fast, as if the point were to arrive somewhere, when the point is precisely not to arrive.

We have largely forgotten how to be aimless. Childhood was full of it, if we were lucky: long afternoons with no structure, turning over rocks, following a cat, building a fort out of sticks and boredom. But adulthood confiscates aimlessness. It tells us that every hour must be optimized, every walk must be exercise, every quiet moment must be filled with an audiobook or a podcast or a carefully curated playlist. Even our leisure has become productive. We rest so we can work better. We walk so we can hit ten thousand steps. We meditate so we can focus. The idea of doing something for no reason, with no measurable outcome, feels almost transgressive.

Yet wandering is one of the oldest human activities. Our ancestors walked not just to hunt or gather, but also to see what was over the next hill. Nomads moved with seasons, but they also moved with curiosity. The philosopher Aristotle was said to teach while walking, his students following him around the Lyceum. The poet Wordsworth composed verses on foot, pacing the Lake District. Friedrich Nietzsche wrote that only thoughts reached on foot have value. There is something about the rhythm of walking that loosens the mind. When the body moves at a certain unhurried pace, thoughts stop marching in straight lines. They begin to drift, spiral, bump into one another. That collision is where creativity lives.

I think of walking as a form of attention. Not the narrow, focused attention of reading a spreadsheet, but a wide, soft attention that takes in everything at once: the smell of rain on hot pavement, the sound of a screen door slamming two blocks away, the particular gray of a pigeon’s wing. This kind of attention is not efficient. It does not filter out the irrelevant. It welcomes the irrelevant. It lets the world press against you without demanding that you extract meaning from it. And in that openness, meaning often arrives on its own, like a cat jumping onto your lap when you stop calling it.

Our current culture of attention is brutally narrow. We scroll, we click, we skim. We consume information in bite-sized pieces and then wonder why we feel starved. The attention economy profits from keeping us in a state of low-grade agitation, always reaching for the next thing, always afraid of missing something. But wandering teaches a different economy. It teaches that attention can be generous rather than grasping. You can look at a thing without needing to photograph it, know its name, or turn it into content. You can simply let it exist and let yourself exist alongside it.

There is a particular kind of loneliness in constant productivity. When every moment is tasked with a purpose, the self becomes a project, always under construction, never quite finished. Wandering offers a reprieve. To wander is to be nobody in particular, going nowhere in particular, and to find that this is enough. It is a small act of trust: trust that the world will offer something worth noticing, trust that your own mind will generate thoughts without being force-fed, trust that an hour spent without achievement is not an hour wasted.

I have been practicing. I leave my phone at home. I choose a direction based on nothing: a street I have never walked down, a bird I want to follow, the way the light is slanting. I let my pace slow until it matches my breathing. At first, there is anxiety. My hands feel empty. My mind keeps reaching for a task. I start mentally drafting emails, reliving conversations, planning dinner. But after about twenty minutes, something shifts. The internal chatter quiets. The world gets louder, or rather, I get quieter enough to hear it. I notice the way tree roots buckle the sidewalk. I notice a child’s drawing taped to a window, a dragon with eight legs and a sun shaped like a potato. I notice the smell of jasmine, so sudden and sweet it feels like a secret.

These walks have taught me that I do not need to fix everything. I do not need to arrive. The pressure to be constantly improving, constantly optimizing, constantly becoming—that pressure is not the natural state of being human. It is a cultural habit, and like all habits, it can be loosened. Wandering is a way of loosening it. It is a quiet refusal to treat your life as a problem to be solved.

I think often of a line by the poet Mary Oliver: “Attention is the beginning of devotion.” If that is true, then wandering is a form of prayer. It is a way of saying to the world: I am here, I am listening, I am not in a hurry. It is a way of loving things not because they are useful, but because they are there. The cracked sidewalk, the overgrown garden, the stranger’s laughter through an open window—these things do not ask for anything. They simply exist, and in their existence they offer a kind of companionship.

There is also something political about wandering. To be aimless in a society that demands purpose is to reject, even if only for an hour, the logic of productivity. It is to say that your worth is not measured by your output. It is to reclaim time as something other than a resource to be spent. This is not laziness. It is a necessary rebalancing. The mind needs fallow periods, just as fields do. Without them, the soil of the imagination becomes depleted. We become efficient but empty.

I have started to notice that my best ideas come when I am not trying to have ideas. They arrive on walks, in the shower, while washing dishes, while staring out a bus window. The common thread is that I am not asking anything of myself. I am simply present, my attention spread wide like a net with no particular fish in mind. The paradox is that this unproductive presence often produces the most valuable things: a new angle on an old problem, a line for a poem, a sudden understanding of someone else’s pain. These gifts cannot be forced. They can only be received.

So I wander. I wander past the corner store with its dusty window displays. I wander through the park where old men play chess on stone tables. I wander down alleys where cats watch me with yellow eyes. I wander until my feet ache and the sky turns the color of a plum. And then I come home, not with a product, not with a proof of my worth, but with a quiet mind and a handful of small, useless, luminous details. It is enough. It is more than enough. It is, I suspect, the whole point.
